column2: That battle was very great and dreadful, scorcher of foes, such as I have never seen before, O lord of men.
Then Kritavarman, O king, pierced Uttamaujas in the heart in the battle, and he sat down on his chariot-seat.
His charioteer carried that best of chariot-warriors away in the chariot, and then swiftly, O king, he went to the Pandava army.
Partha, the hero, with Shauri's help, suddenly checked him as he came on, as the shore holds back the sea.
Then, enraged, O great king, the mighty Drona's son covered Arjuna and Vasudeva with arrows.
The great chariot-warriors there, seeing the two Krishnas covered, fell into utmost wonder and the Kurus looked on.
Then Arjuna, laughing, as it were, brought forth a divine weapon, and the Brahmana in the battle held back that weapon, O Bharata.
Whatever weapon the Pandava hurled in battle to kill him, mighty-bowed Drona's son destroyed each one.
Then, in that terrifying weapon-duel, O king, we saw Drona's son in the battle like Death with gaping mouth.
Covering the quarters and intermediate quarters with straight arrows, he pierced Vasudeva in the right arm with three arrows.
Then Arjuna killed all that great soul's horses and made the ground in the battle a wave-tossed river of blood.
Slain chariot-warriors fell by arrows loosed from Partha's bow, and horses, with traces loosed, ran here and there.
Seeing that deed of Partha, Drona's son, ornament of the battle, covered Krishna on every side with sharp arrows.
Then, O great king, Drona's son, drawing his bow, struck Arjuna in the chest with a feathered arrow in the battle.
Deeply pierced by Drona's son in the battle, O Bharata, he took up a dreadful iron club and hurled it at Drona's son.
As that club adorned with gold came on, Drona's son suddenly cut it, and the people shouted.
It fell to the earth in many pieces by Bharadvaja's son's arrows, like a mountain shattered by the wind, O king.
Then Arjuna in the battle pierced Drona's son with ten arrows and with a broad-headed arrow took his charioteer from the chariot seat.
Taking the reins himself, he covered the two Krishnas with arrows; there we saw the swift valour of Drona's son.
That he controlled the horses and also fought Phalguna—all the warriors there honoured that of his in the battle, O king.
When Phalguna was being swallowed up in the battle by Drona's son, Jaya cut the reins of the chariot horses with razor-arrows.
Those horses fled, afflicted by the force of the arrows, and then a roar of your army arose again, O Bharata.
The Pandavas, having won, rushed at your army, loosing sharp arrows on every side, eager for victory.
The great army of Dhritarashtra's son, O great king, was broken again and again by the Pandava heroes, elated by victory,
in the sight of your sons, the variegated fighters, of Shakuni son of Subala, and of the great-souled Karna.
Though held back by your sons, O lord of men, the great army would not stand in the battle, being struck on all sides.
Then, with the warriors fleeing here and there, O great king, your sons' great force became confused and afraid.
Though the charioteer's son kept saying "Stand, stand!", that army, being slain by the great souls, did not stand.
Then, a shout was raised, O great king, by the victorious Pandavas on seeing Dhritarashtra's army fleeing everywhere.
Then Duryodhana said to Karna, as it were out of affection, "See, Karna, how the army is hard pressed by the Pandavas.
While you stand firm, it flees on all sides in terror. Knowing this, mighty-armed one, do what is fitting, tamer of foes.
Thousands of warriors, O best of men, cry out to you alone in the battle, being routed by the Pandavas."
Hearing Duryodhana's great speech, Radheya, the charioteer's son, said to the king of the Madras:
See the might of my arms and of my weapons, O lord of men; today I shall slay in battle all the Panchalas with the Pandavas; drive the horses, tiger among men, in safety, O lord of men.
Having said this, O great king, the glorious charioteer's son, taking Vijaya, the excellent ancient bow, stringing it and wiping it again and again,
and checking his own warriors with an oath of truth, the immeasurable-souled mighty one applied the Bhargava weapon.
Then, O king, thousands, ten thousands, hundreds of millions and crores of sharp arrows issued in the great battle.
Covered with those dreadful blazing arrows, feathered with heron plumes, the Pandava army could not be made out at all.
A great cry of "Alas" arose among the Panchalas, O lord of men, tormented by the Bhargava weapon in the battle.
With elephants falling, O king, and men by thousands, and chariots too, O tiger among men, and horses on every side,
the earth quaked, O king, with those slain here and there, and the whole great force of the Pandavas became confused.
Karna alone, best of warriors, like a smokeless fire, burning the foes, shone, scorcher of foes.
Slain by Karna, the Panchalas with the Chedis were bewildered here and there like elephants in a forest fire; they cried out, tigers among men, like the best of men before.
Hearing the cries of those frightened ones running at the head of the battle, terrified in all directions, a great cry of distress arose there as of the dead in a flood.
Seeing them slain by the charioteer's son, O revered one, all beings trembled, even those born as animals.
Slain in battle by the charioteer's son, the Srinjayas called repeatedly to Arjuna and Vasudeva, bewildered, as in Yama's city they would call on the king of the dead.
Then Arjuna, son of Kunti, Dhananjaya, said to Vasudeva, seeing the dreadful Bhargava weapon invoked there:

See, Krishna, mighty-armed, the prowess of the Bhargava weapon; this weapon cannot in any way be destroyed in battle.
mahabharata:8:45.47	And see the charioteer's son enraged in the great battle, Krishna, a hero like Death, doing dreadful deeds.
mahabharata:8:45.48	Urging his very swift horses, he looks at me again and again; I do not see Karna fleeing in the battle.
mahabharata:8:45.49	A man alive obtains victory or defeat in battle; but for the defeated, Hrishikesha, there is only death; whence victory?
Then Janardana went, wishing to see Yudhishthira, intending to get Karna to be seized by fatigue in battle, O revered one.
Krishna said to Arjuna, "The king is greatly wounded; comfort him, best of the Kurus, and then you will slay Karna."
Then Dhananjaya went quickly in his chariot to see the king tormented by arrows, at Keshava's command, in the battle.
While going, the son of Kunti, wishing to see the king of dharma, looked over the army and did not see his elder brother there.
Having fought the son of Drona, O Bharata, the son of Kunti, with a swift horse, defeated Bhrigu's son in the battle, hard to endure.
Having defeated Drona's son, the foremost bowman, having done a great, difficult, noble deed, Dhananjaya, unassailable by foes, then surveyed his own army.
As he fought, the heroic Savyasachin cheered the heroes stationed at the head of the host, praising them with famed deeds of old, and made the chariots in the army firm.
Not seeing his elder brother in the fight, the Kiriti spoke to Bhima, the descendant of Ajamidha, who came swiftly: "O king, what is the king's news here?"
[Bhima said:] "The king of dharma Yudhishthira has gone from here, his limbs shattered by Karna's arrows; if he lives at all."
[Arjuna said:] "Therefore go quickly from here for news of the best of the Kurus, the king; surely the king, deeply pierced by Karna's arrows, has gone to the camp.
He who in the night battle, deeply pierced by Drona, the strong one, still stood waiting for victory until Drona was slain,
that foremost Pandava of great power has been brought into peril today in battle by Karna; go quickly, Bhima, to know; I shall stand, holding back the hosts of foes."
[Bhima said:] "Know it for yourself, great one, the news of the king, best of the Bharatas; for if I go there, Arjuna, the heroes will say I am afraid."
Then Arjuna said to Bhimasena, "The Samshaptakas stand opposite me; without slaying them I cannot go from here, from this herd of the enemy host."
Then Bhimasena said to Arjuna, "Relying on my own valour I shall fight all the Samshaptakas in the battle; go, Dhananjaya."
Hearing Bhimasena's hard-to-say words, wishing to see the best of the Kurus among his brother's enemies, he said to the best of the Vrishnis then:
Urge the horses, Hrishikesha, plunging into this sea of chariots; I wish to see King Ajatashatru, Keshava.
Then the chief of the Dasharhas urged the horses and said to Bhima, "This is not wondrous for your deed today, hero; we shall go; slay the hosts of foes, Bhima."
Then Hrishikesha went to where King Yudhishthira was, O king, with horses like Garuda, swifter than swift.
Having placed Bhimasena, tamer of foes, in the opposing front and instructed Vrikodara about the battle, O king of kings,
the two best of men then went and, reaching the king lying alone, both dismounted from the chariot and bowed at the feet of the king of dharma.
Seeing those two tigers among men safe, the best of men, he joyfully welcomed the two Krishnas, as Vasava the two Ashvins.
The king welcomed them as Vivasvat the Ashvins, as Shakra and Vishnu their teacher when the great asura Jambha was slain.
Thinking Karna slain, the king of dharma Yudhishthira, pleased, said to the two tamers of foes in a voice choked with joy:
The son of Kunti welcomed them with sweet, conciliatory words, smiling first, honouring them, O best of the Bharatas, slayer of foes.
[Yudhishthira said:] "Welcome, son of Devaki; welcome, Dhananjaya; your sight is dear to me indeed, Achyuta and Arjuna.
Unwounded and unharmed, how did you fight, great chariot-warriors, him who in battle is like a venomous serpent, skilled in all weapons,
the foremost of Dhritarashtra's men, the shield and armour of his side, guarded by Vrishasena and the archer Sushena,
permitted by Rama, of great valour, hard to conquer in weapons, the protector of Dhritarashtra's sons, the leader at the head of the army,
slayer of the enemy armies, crusher of hosts of foes, devoted to Duryodhana's good, ready to fight us,
unassailable in a great battle even by the gods with Vasava, equal to fire and wind in splendour and strength,

deep as the netherworld, increaser of his friends' joy, like Death to his foes—having slain Karna in the great battle, by good fortune you two have returned, having conquered the asura, like two immortals.
In the sight of Dhrishtadyumna, the twins, the hero Shikhandin, the sons of Draupadi and all the Panchalas,
Karna, having conquered those mighty ones and many hosts of foes, conquered me too, mighty-armed one, as I strove in the great battle.
And, having followed me in the fight, he spoke many harsh words there and there, best of warriors, slighting me, no doubt.
That I live is due to Bhimasena's might, Dhananjaya. What more need be said? I cannot bear that.
Because of him, Dhananjaya, in fear for thirteen years I have not slept at night nor had happiness anywhere by day.
Joined to hatred of him, I burn, Dhananjaya, knowing my own death, like a tusked elephant.
Thinking, lord, how Karna could be destroyed by me in battle, this time has passed for me.
Waking or sleeping, son of Kunti, I always see Karna alone; this world has become Karna.
Wherever I go in fear of Karna, Dhananjaya, there I see Karna standing before me.
That very hero, never fleeing in battle, conquered me with horses and chariot, Partha, and let me go alive.
What use is life to me, or kingdom, thus scorned by Karna, ornament of battle?
What I never received from Bhishma, Kripa or Drona in battle, that I have today received in battle from the charioteer's son, the great chariot-warrior.
Therefore I ask you, son of Kunti, since I am unskilled: tell me fully how Karna was slain by you.
He who was equal to Shakra in valour in battle, like Yama in prowess and like Rama in weapons—how was he slain?
Known as a great chariot-warrior, skilled in all battles, best of archers, the sole man among all,
honoured by Dhritarashtra with his sons, O lord of men, always for you, Radheya—how was he slain by you?
Dhritarashtra among all warriors always thinks, Arjuna, that Karna in battle will be your death, best of men.
How was he slain in battle by you, tiger among men? Tell me, Bibhatsu, how Karna was slain by you.
His proud head, in the sight of his friends, was carried off by you, tiger among men, as a tiger carries off a deer's.
He who attended on all quarters and directions, the charioteer's son, wishing to protect you in battle, desiring to give hosts of elephants—is he now struck by sharp heron-feathered arrows?
Does the charioteer's son, evil-souled, struck down by you in battle, lie on the ground? Have you today done me the greatest pleasure by slaying the charioteer's son in battle?
He who rushed on all sides for your sake, proud, the charioteer's son thinking himself a hero—have you slain him today in the encounter?
He who wished to give a golden chariot yoked with the best elephants to others for your sake and always rivalled you in battle—that sinner, dear one, did you slay him in the battle?
He who, always intoxicated with a hero's pride, boasts in the assembly of the Kauravas and is exceedingly dear to Suyodhana—have you slain that sinner today?
Has that sinner, meeting the arrows loosed from your bow, sent by you, birds that crave blood, fallen with his limbs shattered? Has the arm of Dhritarashtra's son been broken?
He who always boasts in the midst of kings, gladdening Duryodhana, full of pride, 'I shall slay Phalguna'—through delusion, has his chariot been slain?
'I shall never wash my feet so long as Partha stands'—this was always the vow of that small-minded one; has Shakra's son slain Karna today?
He who, ill-minded, said to Krishna in the assembly among the Kuru heroes, 'Why do you not abandon the Pandavas, Krishna, the weak, fallen, spiritless ones?'
And he who vowed for your sake, 'I will not come here without having slain Partha with Krishna'—that sinful-minded Karna, does he lie with his limbs torn by arrows?
Was that meeting known in battle of the Srinjayas and Kauravas in which I was brought to such a state? Have you slain him, meeting him today?
With arrows blazing, loosed from Gandiva, Savyasachin, has that very dull-witted one's head, shining with earrings, been severed from his body in battle by you?
What I meditated for Karna's slaying when I was committed to the arrows, did you today accomplish that meditation of mine, by felling Karna?
He on whom Suyodhana, full of pride, looks at us, relying on Karna—have you broken that support of Suyodhana today by valour?
He who earlier called us sesame seeds of eunuchs in the midst of the assembly of kings, in the presence of kings—has that ill-minded, very impatient charioteer's son been slain in the battle?
He who, laughing, the evil-souled charioteer's son, formerly said, 'She was won by Subala's son; seize Yajnaseni by force and bring her'—has he been slain by you today?
He who with a small mind reviled the Grandsire, best of weapon-bearers on earth, counted as half-chariot-warrior—has Adhiratha's son, the evil-souled, been slain by you today?
This impatient fire seated in my heart, fanned by deceit's wind, always—say, Phalguna, 'He has been slain by me today, meeting him, the evil-minded one,' and quench it."
[Arjuna said:] "While I was fighting the Samshaptakas, O king, Drona's son, leading the Kuru army's van, loosing arrows like venomous serpents, suddenly stood before me.
Seeing this cloud-like chariot of mine, the Ambashtha army stood ready to die; having slain five hundred of them, I then went to Drona's son, best of kings.
Then he loosed masses of other arrows, drawn to the ear and let go with skill, weapon-strength and effort, like a cloud in the rains.
We could not tell when he took or aimed, or with which hand he shot, left or right; that son of Drona turned about in the battle.
Drona's son pierced me with five sharp arrows and Vasudeva with five; I in an instant pierced him with thirty arrows like thunderbolts.
Streaming blood from all his limbs, overcome by me, he entered the chariot-army of the charioteer's son, and I saw him seeing the best of soldiers smeared with blood.
Then, seeing the army overcome in the battle, its warriors shattered, its horses and elephants fleeing, Karna, crusher, with fifty chariot-leaders came swiftly at me.
Having slain them and leaving Karna, I came swiftly to see you; all the Panchalas are terrified of Karna as cattle of the smell of a lion.
The Prabhadrakas run at Karna as into the mouth of a great fish, as if falling into the gaping mouth of Death, O king, reaching Karna.
Come, see me today eager to fight and the charioteer's son, surrounded for victory; six thousand princes, O Bharata, have sunk in their chariots to the heavenly world.
Meeting the charioteer's son in battle, as the thunderbolt-wielder Vritra, O foremost of kings, I shall fight the charioteer's son hard, if he is seen in this battle today.
If I do not slay Karna today, O king, fighting with his kinsmen, forcibly, may I go to the hard fate of those who break their promise, O lion among kings.
I take leave of you; say 'Victory for me in battle'; formerly Dhritarashtra's sons devoured Bhima; I shall slay the son of the charioteer, O lion among kings, his army and all his hosts of foes."
[Yudhishthira said:] "If you had said this in the Dvaita forest—'I cannot withstand Karna in battle, O king'—we would then at once have taken up the course suited to the time, Partha.
Having promised me his slaying and his strength, hero, why did you bring us into the midst of the enemy and then hurl us to the ground and crush us?
We hoped in you, Arjuna, as those wishing to cross hope in an excellent thing; all that is fruitless to us, prince, like an overgrown nichula tree to those wanting fruit.
As a hook is covered with bait, as a wild ox covered with false reproach, you have shown me a useless thing—the ruin of the kingdom in the guise of a kingdom, for one desiring a kingdom.
When the voice in the sky said to Pritha, when you, slow-witted one, were born seven days: 'A son has been born, of Vasava's valour, who will conquer all heroic foes.
He will conquer the hosts of gods at Khandava and all beings; he, of excellent vigour, will conquer the Madrakas, Kalingas and Kekayas; he will slay the Kurus in the midst of kings.
After him there will be no bowman; none has ever conquered him; he, a noble one, could bring all beings under control, self-controlled, with complete knowledge.
In beauty equal to the moon, in speed to the wind, in steadiness to Meru, in forbearance to earth, in radiance to the sun, in fortune to Kubera, in heroism to Shakra, in strength to Vishnu,

your great-souled son of Kunti, like Vishnu born of Aditi, slayer of foes, will be famed for the victory of his own side and the slaying of foes, of immeasurable vigour, the maker of the family line.'
Thus the voice spoke in the sky on the peak of Shatashringa as the ascetics listened. Such as you, that has not come true today; surely the gods speak untruth.
So too hearing the words of other best of sages who ever honour it, he does not come to submission to Suyodhana; I do not know you, afraid of Adhiratha's son.

Having mounted the fair monkey-bannered chariot made by Tvashtri, with silent axles, taking a gold-adorned bright sword and this Gandiva bow of palm-tree length, driven by Keshava, how, Partha, have you left Karna in fear?
Give this bow to Keshava and be charioteer yourself in battle, evil-minded one; then Keshava would slay the fierce Karna, as the lord of the Maruts, thunderbolt in hand, Vritra.
You should have fallen in the fifth month with much pain, or Pritha's womb should not have borne you; then that fatigue would have been yours, prince, not fleeing the battle, evil-souled one."
Seeing his anger, Keshava, knowing his mind, said then, "What is this, Partha? You have taken up a sword!
I see nothing here for you to fight, Dhananjaya; all those sons of Dhritarashtra are destroyed by the wise Bhima.
You came away, son of Kunti, to see the king; King Yudhishthira has been seen by you, well.
Having seen him, a lion among kings, equal in valour to a tiger, when the time of joy has come, why has anger seized you?
I do not see here, son of Kunti, anyone who should be killed by you; why do you take up the great sword in haste?
Therefore I ask you, son of Kunti: what is this that you wish to do, that you, of wondrous valour, enraged, seize a sword?"
Thus addressed by Krishna, looking at Yudhishthira, Arjuna, sighing like an enraged serpent, said to Govinda:

'Give Gandiva to another'—whoever urges me thus, I would cut off his head; that is my secret vow.
mahabharata:8:49.10	That was said to me, firm of heart, by the king of immeasurable valour, in your presence, Govinda, and I cannot bear it here.
mahabharata:8:49.11	Therefore I shall slay this king, fearful of dharma; I shall keep my vow by slaying this best of men; for this, Yadava, I took up the sword.
mahabharata:8:49.12	Having slain Yudhishthira, I shall be free of debt in truth, free of sorrow and fever, Janardana.
mahabharata:8:49.13	Or what do you think proper at this arisen time? You know, dear one, all that this world comes and goes; I shall do as you tell me.

[Krishna said:] "Now I know, Partha, that you have not served the elders. At the wrong time, tiger among men, with this act of fury—one who knows the divisions of dharma would not do thus, Dhananjaya.
He who mixes together what should not be done and what should be done, and what is to be done with what is not to be done, is the lowest of men, Partha.
You do not know the decision of those wise ones who follow dharma and are versed in its brief and detailed forms.
A man who does not know the decision between what is to be done and not done is helpless and bewildered, Partha, as you, who are indeed deluded.
What is to be done and not done is not easily known; all is known through learning, and that you do not understand.
Through ignorance, you who know dharma protect dharma; the righteous does not understand the killing of creatures, Partha.
Non-killing of beings, dear one, is in my view the greatest of all; one may speak an untruth but should never kill.
How would you, best of men, kill your eldest brother, the king, skilled in dharma, like an ordinary man?
Killing one not fighting, weaponless, O Bharata, turned away, fleeing, seeking refuge, with joined palms, or who has surrendered, is not praised by the wise.
And you yourself, Partha, took a vow long ago as a boy; therefore through folly you resolve on a deed joined with unrighteousness.
Why would you, Partha, kill your elder, remembering dharma, without considering the subtle course of the dharmas, so hard to follow?
Throughout that city, from children up, a great cry of distress arose, O tiger among men, on hearing that the king was slain.
It was strewn with waters of many kinds, adorned with pools, covered by hundreds of lotus-ponds and joined with blue lotuses.
Let the Pandavas see me today, firm in vows, set on the long road that opens to the world of Brahma.
The refuge of Dhritarashtra's sons, proud, of keen valour, impatient, ever violent, a reviler of us in battle after battle—
Those who desire the time-bond abandon sorrow at once; those who know the object abandon grief; for those who always grieve, welfare is lost; therefore abandon grief when he is slain.
Not having heard this hero's sweet words, I have obtained great sorrow as the fruit and am sunk in an ocean of grief.
And whatever kings had gathered from all sides, all of them attended on the lord of the Kurus as before.
Thus addressed, those sages then went to Keshava.
Then all the women wept on seeing the bulls among men departing, with Draupadi as sixth, as when long ago they were defeated at dice.
For whose sake the earth was destroyed with horses, chariots and elephants, and we, burnt by anger, wished to take revenge—
